transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-23 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Leo Zhang (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood CSM), Priya Menon (Halcyon VP Eng), Aiden Cole (Halcyon SRE), Samira Khan (Halcyon CISO)

Summary (auto): Follow-up on Mar 18th incident where inference latency spiked and autoscale failed to bring additional capacity; discussed root cause, mitigations, and next steps.

[00:00] Maya Patel: ok, thanks everyone for joining, um today is the follow up for the outage on the 18th, we've pulled logs and I want to walk through the timeline and the fixes, uh Leo will take technical deep dive after i set context
[00:18] Priya Menon: thanks Maya, appreciate it, we had a big customer incident, svc divers in production started seeing 5xx and 10s of seconds latency, that hour cost us several robot control cycles so big impact
[00:35] Leo Zhang: yeah hi all, quick note — transcription might flip some names, but i'll try to be clear, root cause summary: interplay between our autoscaler and the customer's long-lived KV cache invalidation during a model swap caused sustained queuing; autoscaler threshold bounced and didn't fully replenish pods in time
[00:55] Aiden Cole: when you say model swap, do you mean the rolling update you did the morning of the 18th? we saw a spike right at 09:12 UTC
[01:10] Leo Zhang: yes, exactly, there was a rolling rollout to a quantized variant, that triggered cache invalidation for KV cache entries; many, many warmup misses — the initial prefix cache miss rate was in the high 90s
[01:28] Samira Khan: can you clarify KV cache? is that redwood's kv cache or our redis? we have redis for session state
[01:38] Leo Zhang: good q. this is Redwood's in-memory KV cache used for prefix/kv key-values for transformer caching, not your redis — sorry if docs weren't clear on that, we should call it out more explicitly
[01:52] Priya Menon: ok, that distinction helps; so warmup misses flooded the inference queue and the autoscaler judged it as steady load rather than transient spike?
[02:06] Leo Zhang: roughly — our autoscaler uses a request lat percentile and queued work metric; because the warmup churn produced a sustained CPU/queue signal across all nodes, the autoscaler started adding nodes but there was an interplay with our pod startup time on the Dedicated pool and the model artifact pull time, so there was a 3-6 min lag window where requests queued and latency spiked
[02:31] Carlos Ruiz: to add, during that window some fallback logic tried to route to a cheaper hosted model variant but the customer's routing policy had a strict allowlist (private-only) so fallback was blocked, which exacerbated failures
[02:49] Priya Menon: we did have that allowlist for data residency, yes — are you saying the fallback would have helped if allowed?
[02:58] Leo Zhang: it would have reduced peak latency and 5xx by serving on a compatible hosted variant, yes, but i totally appreciate the policy constraints
[03:12] Priya Menon: okay that makes sense.
[03:18] Maya Patel: quick pause — i want to cover what we did immediately post-incident: we pushed a temporary config lock to prevent aggressive cache eviction, manually warmed the KV cache by replaying recent prefixes, and increased scale-up aggressiveness for that Dedicated pool. we also opened a ticket to improve model pull parallelism.
[03:42] Aiden Cole: the manual warm sounds good, did you run into any memory pressure doing that? our nodes are fairly memory constrained
[03:52] Leo Zhang: we were cautious — warmed in 2 phases to avoid OOMs, so memory delta was about 8-12% for the pool, under the node headroom, but noted for future we can do streaming/warmup-to-disk to reduce memory spike
[04:10] Samira Khan: security note — when you warmed caches and pulled artifacts, any private weights were exposed outside our VPC? we need assurances about artifact transport and KMS usage
[04:22] Maya Patel: good point, Samira — all artifact pulls were within the customer's private deployment, authenticated with their KMS-managed keys; we did not transfer model weights to Redwood-hosted buckets. we'll include transport logs in the artifacts we share
[04:36] Samira Khan: please include the KMS key IDs and the audit trail, and the SSO SAML assertion logs if possible
[04:45] Carlos Ruiz: noted, we'll attach the audit logs to the incident packet.
[04:50] Priya Menon: can we walk through the proposed remediation and long-term fixes?
[04:55] Leo Zhang: sure — technical fixes we recommend: 1) implement a config lock around KV cache invalidation to avoid full-cache blowouts during model swaps; 2) improve autoscaler heuristics to weight cold-warm cache signals differently from sustained client load; 3) add staggered model pull and prefetching during rollouts; 4) provide a fallback policy shim that allows temporary cross-variant routing for emergency recovery while respecting data residency via encryption in transit
[05:28] Aiden Cole: heuristic change sounds good but how invasive is that to the runtime?
[05:33] Leo Zhang: moderate — mostly in the autoscaler tuning layer and request router; runtime changes are small but need QA. we can push heuristics as a config toggle first for Halcyon to test.
[05:46] Priya Menon: about the fallback shim — we can't accept data leaving our VPC, but if you can guarantee encryption and ephemeral instance tenancy tied to our TID, that might work. Samira?
[05:58] Samira Khan: maybe — I'd need to see threat model and KMS flow, but ephemeral tenancy and E2E encryption + audit logs could be acceptable for emergency only
[06:12] Maya Patel: we'll prepare a proposed secure fallback design doc and share by Friday.
[06:18] Carlos Ruiz: operationally, we also want to propose a canary rollout pattern and a checklist before any model swap: pre-warm sample prefixes, run canary in small percentage of traffic, and stagger nodes to avoid mass invalidation
[06:33] Priya Menon: that is exactly what we want, checklist and pre-warm step, plus canary gate before broad rollout.
[06:41] Leo Zhang: on the perf side, we also found a regression in our kernel selection for the quantized variant that increased CPU decode time by ~12% for certain sequence patterns — not the primary root cause but contributed to longer pull/initialization times
[06:58] Aiden Cole: regression? was that in the 1.8 runtime?
[07:03] Leo Zhang: yes, introduced during the 1.8 kernel selection changes; we have a patch and will backport to the Dedicated runtime branch, will include the PR link in the report
[07:16] Priya Menon: would that patch require a restart of the entire pool? we can't afford downtime outside maintenance windows
[07:23] Leo Zhang: patch can be rolled as a rolling update with canary; no full outage needed, but pre-warm must be included as part of the rollout checklist
[07:32] Samira Khan: we also want clarity around alerting, the SREs said they didn't get a clear escalation path and the paging thresholds were too noisy
[07:42] Carlos Ruiz: thanks, we'll revise the on-call playbook and escalation matrix. Maya will send the updated contacts.
[07:49] Maya Patel: yep, i'll send updated escalation matrix and on-call contacts after this call.
[07:55] Aiden Cole: something else — is there an easy way for us to run the exact failing workload in Redwood sandbox to reproduce without touching prod?
[08:04] Leo Zhang: yes, we can spin up a Dedicated sandbox with pinned model and same traffic profile; ideally we get your sample payloads and replay scripts, then we can run deterministic repros and tweak autoscaler there
[08:22] Priya Menon: we'll provide the payloads. expect to upload to your secure share by Thursday.
[08:28] Maya Patel: perfect. next on the agenda — timeline and checkpoints. Carlos, do you want to propose dates?
[08:35] Carlos Ruiz: proposed: by 2027-03-25 we deliver incident packet (logs, audit, timeline), by 2027-03-26 SE to run perf benchmarks on dedicated sandbox and share results, by 2027-03-30 security Q&A and fallback design doc, then a remediation rollout window week of 2027-04-04 for canary rollout.
[08:55] Priya Menon: that works for us. any blockers?
[09:00] Samira Khan: only if we don't get the KMS/audit IDs in time — need those to sign off on fallback design
[09:08] Maya Patel: we will include KMS key IDs in the packet on 3/25.
[09:12] Aiden Cole: small note about cost — you mentioned more aggressive scaling and pre-warm, that will cost us more; can we get an estimate?
[09:20] Leo Zhang: yes we'll add cost delta estimates for pre-warm and canary. expect a small incremental monthly cost for warmed buffer and faster scale-ups, we'll quantify in the packet
[09:30] Priya Menon: regarding the autoscaler heuristic change, can we do a toggle we control, so we can experiment without broad impact?
[09:38] Leo Zhang: absolutely — config toggle per-customer is our plan. we'll push heuristics as opt-in configuration for Halcyon first.
[09:46] Maya Patel: ok let's capture action items — (1) incident packet and timeline (Carlos/Maya) due 3/25; (2) perf run in sandbox (Leo) due 3/26 with results; (3) remediation/canary plan (Carlos) due 3/25; (4) security docs and fallback design (Maya/Leo) due 3/30; (5) customer to provide replay payloads and logs (Priya) due 3/24
[10:20] Priya Menon: sounds good, appreciate the quick follow up.
[10:25] Samira Khan: thanks, also we'll schedule internal compliance review after we get the artifact packet.
[10:32] Maya Patel: thank you all. we'll follow up in email with the links to the incident packet and the sheet for scheduling the perf run.
[10:40] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional misrecognition of product names (e.g., "Redwood Dedicat"), speaker overlap in Q&A; timestamps approximate.
